meta.title: From scattered updates to clear decisions
meta.subtitle: A practical operating model for project reviews
meta.author: Alex Morgan
meta.centralClaim: A project review should produce a decision, not another status summary.

content.heading: The meeting ended. What changed?
content.lead: If nobody can name the decision, the review was only a report.

notes.say: Think about your last project review. You heard updates, saw several charts, and probably discussed risks. But what decision did the meeting produce?

content.heading: Ambiguity creates work after the meeting
content.lead: People leave with different interpretations, so the team pays twice.

notes.say: The numbers are illustrative, but the pattern is common. A vague review creates follow-up messages, side meetings, and rework. The important number is zero: no decision recorded.

content.heading: Evidence should lead to a named decision
content.lead: Use the same sequence for every review.

notes.say: Start with the signal that matters. Put the real choice on the screen. Name one owner, then set a date. Four steps are enough for most project reviews.

content.heading: Design each slide around the decision
content.lead: The slide becomes a working surface for the room.

items.title: What changed?
items.text: Show the new signal, not a full history.

items.title: What is the choice?
items.text: Write the options in plain language.

items.title: Who acts next?
items.text: Name the owner before leaving the slide.

notes.do: Ask the audience which question is usually missing.
notes.say: These questions make a review useful. Most teams are good at explaining what changed. Fewer make the choice explicit, and ownership often arrives in a follow-up message.

content.heading: Put the decision in the slide title
content.lead: Test the model in one real meeting this week.

items: Rewrite one status title as a decision question.
Name the owner before the meeting ends.
Record the choice and date in the same place.

notes.say: Try this in one real review. Rewrite a status title as the decision the room must make. If that changes the conversation, keep the model.
